subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Pseudoscience: What Science Isn't
description: A short lesson to help you apply Pseudoscience: What Science Isn't.

hook.text: Astrology, homeopathy, & crystal healing all claim to be scientific.

buildup.text: Pseudoscience mimics the appearance of science — jargon, citations, lab coats — without the substance.

discovery.text: Red flags: unfalsifiable claims, reliance on anecdotes, conspiracy theories about suppression, & no peer-reviewed.

twist.text: The line isn't always clear. Some fields hover at the boundary — they may become science with better evidence.

climax.text: The demarcation problem (Popper): distinguishing science from pseudoscience is one of philosophy's hardest questions.

punchline.text: If it looks like science but can't be tested, it's wearing a costume.

quiz.question: What is the biggest red flag that something is pseudoscience?
options: Its claims cannot be tested or falsified

details.summary: Pseudoscience mimics the language and appearance of science without following its methods. It avoids falsifiable claims, cherry-picks evidence, and appeals to authority rather than empirical testing.
details.whyItMatters: Pseudoscience is dangerous precisely because it looks like science. Learning to tell the difference protects you from harmful advice dressed in a lab coat.
takeaways: Pseudoscience uses scientific language without scientific methodology
It avoids falsifiable predictions and resists correction
Red flags include appeals to ancient wisdom and conspiracy claims about suppression

faq.question: What are the clearest red flags that something is pseudoscience?
faq.answer: Claims that cannot be tested, reliance on testimonials over controlled studies, hostility toward legitimate criticism, appeals to conspiracy when evidence is lacking, and failure to update when contradicted by evidence.

faq.question: Why is the boundary between science and pseudoscience sometimes blurry?
faq.answer: Emerging fields may lack established test methods. Historical science sometimes got things wrong initially. The key difference is attitude toward evidence: science welcomes correction while pseudoscience resists it.
